scenes.visual: Title card 'Why the Trade-off Hides'. COLOUR MAP, the same in both films and on the page: BLACK bar = intake (A), what one animal takes in; GOLD = reproduction (R); TEAL = self (S: growth, upkeep, storage, drawn as teal sub-bands when split out); GREY = trend lines and labels. Axes, when shown: horizontal = GOLD reproduction R, vertical = TEAL self S. The songbird is the same small great-tit-like cartoon in both films; the salmon icon matches the lesson's semelparity figure. Cream background, 16:9. Every number appears only as on-screen text. Cartoons and labelled blocks only, no molecular structures; anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: The first film gave every bird the same intake. If breeding can cost a bird its future, why do birds that lay more eggs often survive better? At first glance, breeding looks good for them.
scenes.visual: The first film's trade-off line returns (GOLD R horizontal, TEAL S vertical, slope -1). Then the line fades and a scatter of real-looking dots appears, labelled 'clutch size' (horizontal) and 'parent survival to next year' (vertical), sloping UP, with caption 'larger clutches, better survival'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: The first film gave every bird the same intake. If breeding can cost a bird its future, why do birds that lay more eggs often survive better? At first glance, breeding looks good for them.

scenes.tts: Draw the line for a poor bird. Its intake is small, so its line sits close to the corner. A rich bird takes in more. Its line sits further out, with the same downward slope. Same split, more of both.
scenes.visual: A short BLACK intake bar and its trade-off line near the origin, labelled 'poor bird'. A long BLACK bar and a parallel line further out, labelled 'rich bird'. Each bird's dot sits at the same split (middle of its line), so the rich bird's dot is higher on BOTH axes: caption 'same split, more of both'.
scenes.narration: Draw the line for a poor bird. Its intake is small, so its line sits close to the corner. A rich bird takes in more. Its line sits further out, with the same downward slope. Same split, more of both.

scenes.tts: Now fill in a whole population. Each bird is a dot on its own line, and every line slopes down. Yet birds that take in more sit further out on both axes. So the cloud of dots slopes up.
scenes.visual: Computed: 60 parallel trade-off lines, one per bird, intakes drawn at random (mean 10, spread 30%), each with a dot at a split near one half (spread 0.02). The thin lines all slope down in faint grey; the dots form a cloud, and a GREY trend line through the cloud slopes UP. Label 'every line slopes down; the cloud slopes up'.
scenes.narration: Now fill in a whole population. Each bird is a dot on its own line, and every line slopes down. Yet birds that take in more sit further out on both axes. So the cloud of dots slopes up.

scenes.tts: Van Noordwijk and de Jong made this point in nineteen eighty-six. People with large incomes tend to have bigger houses and newer cars. Yet for any one income, money spent on the house is not there for the car.
scenes.caption: Van Noordwijk and de Jong made this point in 1986. People with large incomes tend to have bigger houses and newer cars. Yet for any one income, money spent on the house is not there for the car.
scenes.visual: Three people icons with income bars of different lengths; each bar splits into a house and a car, both growing with income. Then zoom on one bar: a slider moves money from car to house, and the car shrinks as the house grows. Caption 'van Noordwijk and de Jong, 1986'.
scenes.narration: Van Noordwijk and de Jong made this point in 1986. People with large incomes tend to have bigger houses and newer cars. Yet for any one income, money spent on the house is not there for the car.

scenes.tts: So a positive natural correlation does not refute a trade-off. It may simply reflect who took in more. To test the trade-off, change breeding effort on purpose.
scenes.visual: The upward cloud returns. A red 'trade-off refuted?' stamp appears and is crossed out. Then caption 'test: change effort at random'.
scenes.narration: So a positive natural correlation does not refute a trade-off. It may simply reflect who took in more. To test the trade-off, change breeding effort on purpose.

scenes.tts: Here is how. Take a set of nests. At random, add two chicks to half of them, and leave the other half alone. Parents of enlarged broods now have more mouths to feed.
scenes.visual: A row of 12 cartoon nests. A coin icon flips over each; half receive two extra GOLD chick icons ('enlarged'), half do not ('control'). Small label: 'schematic: parents may also forage harder'.
scenes.narration: Here is how. Take a set of nests. At random, add two chicks to half of them, and leave the other half alone. Parents of enlarged broods now have more mouths to feed.

scenes.tts: Because a coin chose the nests, rich and poor parents are balanced between the groups on average. A later difference in parent survival can then be laid on the extra chicks, allowing for chance.
scenes.visual: The enlarged and control groups are shown as two piles of bird icons; each pile holds a mix of long and short BLACK intake bars. Caption 'random assignment: rich and poor parents balanced on average'.
scenes.narration: Because a coin chose the nests, rich and poor parents are balanced between the groups on average. A later difference in parent survival can then be laid on the extra chicks, allowing for chance.

scenes.tts: Now a question for you. Suppose extra chicks cost parents some survival. What should happen to the parents of enlarged broods by the next spring? Will more of them come back, fewer, or the same?
scenes.visual: A spring calendar page turns. The two groups of parents wait under a large question mark; return counts are hidden behind grey boxes.
scenes.narration: Now a question for you. Suppose extra chicks cost parents some survival. What should happen to the parents of enlarged broods by the next spring? Will more of them come back, fewer, or the same?

scenes.visual: Hold on the question mark; a 5-second ring timer counts down.

scenes.tts: A meta-analysis gathered such studies across thirty bird species. On average, parents of enlarged broods survived a little less well. The cost per extra chick was uncertain. And a cost could also fall on later breeding, not survival. In the same data, birds with naturally larger clutches survived better. Two opposite signs, which fits the cloud, though it does not prove it.
scenes.caption: A meta-analysis gathered such studies across 30 bird species. On average, parents of enlarged broods survived a little less well. The cost per extra chick was uncertain. And a cost could also fall on later breeding, not survival. In the same data, birds with naturally larger clutches survived better. Two opposite signs, which fits the cloud, though it does not prove it.
scenes.visual: On-screen text '30 bird species (eLife, 2025)'. Two arrows side by side: 'enlarged broods: parent survival' with a short downward GOLD arrow labelled 'small, uncertain', and 'naturally larger clutches: parent survival' with an upward GREY arrow. The upward cloud returns behind them.
scenes.narration: A meta-analysis gathered such studies across 30 bird species. On average, parents of enlarged broods survived a little less well. The cost per extra chick was uncertain. And a cost could also fall on later breeding, not survival. In the same data, birds with naturally larger clutches survived better. Two opposite signs, which fits the cloud, though it does not prove it.

scenes.tts: So a natural correlation alone cannot show a trade-off, or rule one out. Birds that take in more can do better at everything. Adding chicks at random tests what extra breeding costs. And each bird may still face its own downward line.
scenes.visual: Left: the upward cloud with caption 'correlation alone: ambiguous'. Right: the enlarged and control groups side by side with caption 'random change: tests the cost'.
scenes.narration: So a natural correlation alone cannot show a trade-off, or rule one out. Birds that take in more can do better at everything. Adding chicks at random tests what extra breeding costs. And each bird may still face its own downward line.

scenes.visual: End card with the hexagon mascot: 'Natural correlations can hide a trade-off; random manipulation tests the cost.'
